summary.title: Transparent Hugepage Support
summary.one_liner: Learn how the Linux kernel's Transparent Hugepage (THP) feature works, and how to control it via sysfs, prctl, madvise, boot parameters, khugepaged, and /proc counters.
keywords: how to enable transparent huge pages linux
reduce tlb misses with larger pages
takeaways: THP automatically backs anonymous memory and tmpfs/shmem with huge pages, without the reservation model of hugetlbfs, and can be restricted system-wide, per task, or per memory range.
Global controls in /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/ (enabled and defrag, plus per-size hugepages-<size>kB settings) choose always, madvise, never, or defer behaviour.
khugepaged collapses runs of base pages into huge pages; its knobs (pages_to_scan, scan_sleep_millisecs, max_ptes_none, max_ptes_swap, max_ptes_shared) tune how aggressive it is.
Monitor THP usage via AnonHugePages and ShmemHugePages in /proc/meminfo, per-process smaps, and /proc/vmstat counters such as thp_fault_alloc and thp_fault_fallback.
summary.summary: This is the official Linux kernel admin guide page describing Transparent Hugepage Support. It explains the performance rationale (fewer page faults and fewer TLB misses), the newer multi-size THP (mTHP) feature, and the trade-off that huge pages can waste memory for sparsely touched regions. It then documents the sysfs controls for enabled, defrag, use_zero_page and shrink_underused, the khugepaged tuning knobs, process-level prctl controls, boot parameters for anon, shmem and tmpfs policies, and the meminfo and vmstat counters used for monitoring.
